This was a scrutiny session with a focus on higher and further education. Kirsty Williams, Cabinet Secretary for Education, Eluned Morgan, Minister for Welsh Language and Lifelong Learning, and Huw Morris, who was the group director of skills, higher education and lifelong learning. The first questions were from Suzy Davies. She wanted to know whether there's still a problem recruiting teachers into the 300 priority places, or is there a trend where things are getting better? Then, the committee discussed the issue of those websites that offer to write essays for cash. They agreed that it was a terrible and abhorrent practice in the system, and they would do everything they could to work with colleagues across the United Kingdom to find a solution to this.

According to Kirsty Williams, there was still a job of work to do to understand and respond to those needs. First of all, making sure that their ITE provision was world class, so that, actually, Welsh centres were the place to go to train to be a teacher. Secondly, they were trying to follow up on the employment-based routes into qualified teacher status, which were people who were training on the job. Moreover, they had added new incentives this year, both for people starting their course and then for teachers who complete their QTS after a year.

According to Kirsty Williams, there were actually 130 qualifiers who could have gone on to teach in Welsh-medium schools, but they were not necessarily doing a course that gave them that designation. They had initially done some work in the last year specifically targeting Welsh students in studying for priority subject degrees, e-mailing them, sending them materials to ask them to consider (1) becoming a teacher, and (2) crucially coming to do that training here in Wales. They were now part of a full national programme of ITE-recruitment, giving people that idea that you could serve your nation and your community by training to be a teacher. There were still a lot of work to do to understand and respond to those needs, but the government was putting in place plans to improve the situation.

According to Hefin David, Kirsty Williams admitted that there was no one thing that they could do that would solve the problem, but it was an international issue. The accreditation process, which was independent of the Government, demanded of the ITE providers that their provision would be able to meet the goals of the curriculum. The curriculum was very clear about the equality of the language and the ability of the children, through all stages of their education journey, to be able-bodied bilingual children. Therefore, it had to be a UK approach.

According to Kirsty, the process was independent of Government, and it would not be appropriate for him to comment on that. The accreditation process demanded of the ITE providers that their provision would be able to meet the goals of the curriculum. The curriculum was very clear about the equality of the language and the ability of the children, through all stages of their education journey, to be bilingual children.

From the very outset of the ITE reforms, Kirsty Williams had made it clear that he expected very high standards in the system, but the process was independent of this Government. He had confidence in the people who had been appointed by the EWC to undertake the accrediting process, but he did not have any concerns that they would not be in a position to commission the appropriate number of training places as a result of their planning.

Currently, with the current providers, there was a significant geographical spread. There were centres here in the south-east, there were centres in mid Wales, and in north Wales. Obviously, accessibility was an issue for them. Therefore, they were responding with their part-time PGCE route, which actually would be location neutral, because they would be able to study that as a distance learner, and so they were able to remain in their community and undertake that course. So, if geographical disadvantage was stopping somebody from pursuing a career aspiration to qualify as a teacher, their new PGCE, as I said, would allow them to do that.

Hefin David pointed out that Cardiff Metropolitan University was under pressure from the then Minister to merge with the University of Glamorgan and Newport. However, Kirsty Williams insisted that there was no formal policy for reconfiguration or mergers. These were autonomous institutions. If they saw an advantage, they would hope for the student first, and, if they put the student at the front of this process, then they would obviously have an interest in that and making sure that that was the right thing to do.

According to Hefin David, Kirsty Williams was in favor of a healthy, strong and sustainable HE sector. However, he did not have a burning desire or a set policy to pursue mergers. If individual institutions felt that was of benefit to them and their students, obviously, they would have an interest in that and making sure that they were robust plans, but that was a matter for individual institutions.

Kirsty Williams was not aware of any disadvantage to Cardiff Met. He was heartened by some of the really interesting collaborative work that Cardiff Met were interested in doing, and new partnerships and new collaborations between institutions, whether that be Cardiff Uni or local colleges, which were to be welcomed. However, he did not foresee them changing that policy.

This was the Children, Young People and Education Committee's last formal meeting before the new Senedd. It was mainly about the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on health and social services as they relate to children and young people in Wales. The meeting started with a question from Siân Gwenllian, who wanted to know why parents and carers might not take their children into the healthcare system for other conditions while the coronavairus pandevirus was with them. The Minister answered that they had thought again about how to provide the service and how to protect staff and families and the very clear message to parents was to please make sure that when health and care professionals were calling to help and support their family, please discuss their concerns with them, and they were doing even more remotely, via telephone and online. Next, the meeting moved on to discuss the situation of parents refusing to engage with the service. The minister explained that they were aware that there were some sectors in the childcare sector that did fall through some of the loops and they had guaranteed that they would pay the money for the childcare offer for three months, but they were still having to look at their own commutation strategy in relation to that.

According to Vaughan Gething, they still have seven-day-a-week crisis care. They have also been looking at how that's provided on a phone or online basis where possible, because the same concerns exist about physical contact with people. They know there is still more to go. They're still committed to it, but they're concerned about the time frame.

According to Vaughan Gething, the mental health recovery plan would have to be informed by the understanding of what was happening when they got more engagement with families about the level of need, and then how they needed to think about that. In all of the unknowns within this, the impact on mental health and well-being was absolutely one of them, because they were looking at how they then developed not just a recovery plan for the economy but a comprehensive recovery plan around mental health, how they support people, and that would be informed when they had more contact with families.

Tracey Breheny said that there had been some movement around health boards, particularly where in the first phase of the epidemic the concentration was on in-patient provision, providing critical care, but according to the latest tool, those staff were gradually not just returning to work from self-isolation or whatever, or from different parts of the system. There were some discharges of young people, but they had the assurance that that was only undertaken where it was clinically safe to do so and where the community support was in place.

The group talked about the evaluations on the increasing suicide crimes during the COVID-19 and the long-term special care for the pregnant women. The first thing they did was to commission a review to be carried out with the current numbers of unexpected deaths that they had, so they were able to provide a report to understand where they were. Then they commissioned a national advisory group to review the current, unexpected deaths during the start of the pandemic, because they wanted to try to understand the wider concerns about the potential effects of the restrictions on the mental health and well-being of children and young people, and if that was leading to a spike in suicide or not.

According to Vaughan Gething, they still had seven-day-a-week crisis care for children and young people who needed them at the moment. They had built up those crisis care services over a period of time, and the last thing they did not want to see was to see them disappear during this period when there were well-understood concerns about emotional and mental health. They were not services to be scaled down.

According to Vaughan Gething, the perinatal mental health service had not been stopped either. They had been looking at how that was provided on a phone or online basis where possible, because again the same concerns existed about physical contact with people. They knew there was still more to go. They were still committed to it, but they were concerned about the time frame. It was about making sure that people had alternative means that they were prepared to use at this point in time.

Julie Morgan said that the definition of vulnerable children and young people included those with a social worker and with statements of special educational needs, and the most vulnerable of these should be prioritised. However, there were other children who were not necessarily known to services but could still be vulnerable. Therefore, they were giving discretion to the local authorities in order to have a degree of flexibility, and they were working with the third sector.

Julie Morgan thought that it was difficult to monitor if there was not easy access to the children that they were referring to, and that's why they had been trying to encourage the vulnerable children to go into school or childcare settings. The Minister, the director of education and the managing director of social services sent out a joint letter recently to all the local authorities, asking them to try to encourage vulnerable children and the families to get the Children to go to school. This was being dealt with on a case-by-case basis, so every case that was known was being RAG rated and services were being linked to that. Also, there were weekly meetings between officials and the heads of the children's services.

Julie Morgan mentioned that they had worked with the fostering organizations. They had had close communications with them, and they supported AFA Cymru to develop guidance for foster carers, and that guidance had been very strongly welcomed across the sector. They were also working with the third sector. The Fostering Network had extended its helpline hours, and Voices from Care had developed this particular offer of support for care leavers. And the young people appeared to be more stable now, so that was online help for them.

According to Julie Morgan, the Welsh government had not introduced any easements in relation to children's services legislation. Therefore, from a Welsh context, the standards that were in place did remain, so therefore there wouldn't have been a necessity for them to do a children's rights impact assessment. However, according to Albert Heaney, it was still a strong point to them in Wales, both in terms of safeguarding arrangements, but also ensuring that Children's rights were protected at a crucial time.

According to the online survey, thousands of children were asked to give their opinions in terms of what had happened, what they had been doing, and their views on the whole COVID-19 situation. Based on their responses, the team decided to conduct an online survey in conjunction with the children's commissioner, the Young Wales and the Youth Parliament to get feedback from young people.

Heaney believed that from a Welsh context, the standards that were in place did remain, so therefore there wouldn't have been a necessity for them to do a children's rights impact assessment in relation to the primary legislation. Moreover, the coronavirus Act itself was UK Government legislation and they ran their own impact assessments, but in terms of how they implemented it in the childcare and education space, they definitely would be looking at those impacts in terms going forward.

This was the first hybrid meeting of the House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic. Some members were participating via video conference and some were participating in person. In order to ensure that those joining the meeting via video conferees could be seen and heard by those in the chamber, two screens had been set up in the Chamber on either side of the Speakers chair. The meeting started with questions to ministers. The first question was from the Leader of the Opposition, Andrew Scheer. The opposition party demanded that the government implement a universal health care system that did not include the provision of necessary prescription medications. The government promised to implement a system of universal national pharmacare, bringing down the cost of drugs through bulk purchasing.

The Prime Minister argued that from the beginning of this pandemic, the government did need to move extremely quickly, and that's what they did. Eight million Canadians had had that as a replacement for paycheques lost because of COVID-19. They also moved forward on the wage subsidy and a range of other programs to support workers and small businesses. What they had done in terms of helping small businesses with the Canada emergency business account had had a massive impact on small businesses across Canada, but they understood that certain companies and businesses had particularities that meant it was a little more difficult for them to qualify.

The opposition party and the Prime Minister commented about companies laying off workers in the midst of pandemic. The Prime Minister said that the priority had been to be here for workers in difficulty so that they did not lose their jobs. However, the opposition party pointed out that during the pandemic, the government had given money to companies that didn't pay a cent in tax because they used tax havens. The opposition party argued that this was not a big deal.

The issue of long-term care was brought up after the release of the military report detailing the appalling conditions experienced by seniors in the care homes in Ontario. The opposition party argued that the for-profit model was failing the seniors and putting profits ahead of the well-being of seniors. The government argued that it was the duty of the government to support the provinces and territories to ensure that every elder person in the community could age with dignity and in safety.

Hon. Patty Hajdu introduced that Canada had the worst record of COVID-19 deaths in long-term care among 14 comparable countries, with over 80% of Canadian fatalities occurring in these facilities. The report from the Canadian Armed Forces showed appalling conditions, horrific care that was being given to the clients, and also the way that the staff conducted themselves. It was painfully clear that corporate profits were being put ahead of the well-being of seniors. Hon. Bill Blair explained that the government was committed to working with the provinces and territories to ensure that every elder person in the community could age with dignity and in safety.

The opposition party raised the issue that the Minister of Digital Government had been promoting a fundraising campaign to sue Global News for their story criticizing the Chinese Communist Party. The opposition party argued that the minister was using her authority to support the Communist Party of China and threatening the media and freedom of expression. The minister argued that it was very important to protect employees across the country and in every economic sector that's experiencing a significant drop in income.

Hon. Bill Morneau introduced that the government was going to roll out a series of measures to reduce the deficit, including wage subsidy, wage subsidy for workers and small businesses, wage increase for the oil and gas sector, wage reduction for foreign direct investment, and a range of other programs.

The opposition party argued that the U.K. would begin applying tariffs at the beginning of next year on Canadian exports such as seafood, beef and cars, which were the items that had had tariffs removed under CETA. The minister explained that the government was monitoring the situation very carefully and was in discussions with the UK government to see if CETA would continue to apply to the trade with the country during this period while they went through Brexit. However, the opposition party questioned that the minister did not give an exact answer to this question and only promised to publish the objectives of any new trade agreement in the near future.

Hon. Chrystia Freeland (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Intergovernmental Affairs) introduced that Canada had an excellent assurance of its trade with the United States, which was the new NAFTA trade agreement that they had negotiated, thanks to the unprecedented co-operation across this country. It was also important to the Canadian economy and Canadian producers that the government had operated in a very urgent way in order to procure supplies for front-line health care workers in this time of crisis to ensure that the supply chains would remain open. However, it was challenged by Randy Hoback that China was procuring and hoarding PPE. Hon. Anita Anand (Minister of Public Services and Procurement) explained that the Government of Canada's approach was to diversify supply chains internationally and build up and retool domestic industry so that Canada could have these supplies going forward.

Hon. Patty Hajdu (Minister of Health) explained that from the very beginning of the outbreak in early January, the government was aware of the challenges the health sector would face, and they immediately began to work with the provinces and territories to understand what the need would be and how they could best prepare. However, senior Canadian bureaucrats received very credible reports that China was procuring and hoarding PPE. Therefore, the minister explained that the government had been procuring goods aggressively in domestic and international markets.

During the pandemic, the government gave money to Air Canada, but Air Canada never reimbursed customers who did not get the services they paid for. During the same period, the Liberals used the emergency wage subsidy to fund partisan activities. The Minister of National Revenue promised that in everything they do, they would target companies and not innocent workers.

Hon. Patty Hajdu introduced that the government had started the steps some four years ago or so when it began to make incredible investments in aging at home. Now, the government was working with the provinces and territories to make sure that they had a longer-term plan so that all seniors could age with dignity and safety. However, as the member opposite pointed out, the jurisdiction for care of long-term care homes fell within the provincial and territorial realm. Therefore, it was important for the government to work with all the provinces, territories, and the federal government to ensure that every elder person in the community could age safely and with dignity.

Hon. Patty Hajdu introduced that COVID-19 had exposed critical vulnerabilities across Canada's entire network of long-term care facilities. Not a single province or territory currently met the benchmark of 4.1 hours of hands-on care per day. As a result Canada had the worst record of COVID19 deaths in seniors care among 14 comparable countries, with over 80% of Canadian fatalities occurring in these facilities. The Prime Minister promised to work with the provinces and territories to ensure that every elder person in the community could age with dignity and in safety.

This was the Children, Young People and Education Committee meeting. It was mainly about the evidence session on the higher education new academic year allocations.
